contents.name: Section 1.2 'Newtonian Mechanics: A Single Particle': a particle as an object of insignificant size, F = dp/dt with F(r,r-dot), p = m r-dot, and the caveat that the equation holds only in an inertial frame, defined by r = r_0 + v t for a free particle
Section 1.2: the ten transformations between inertial frames (3 rotations r' = O r with orthogonal O, 3 translations, 3 boosts r' = r + u t, 1 time translation) generating the Galilean group
Section 1.2.1 angular momentum L = r x p and torque, Sections 1.2.2-1.2.3 conservation laws and energy, Section 1.2.4 examples
contents.reason: The balance laws and their examples belong to the momentum/work/energy pages of the classical mechanics track, which own their own definitions (centre of mass, potential, kinetic energy) and hypotheses; the framework page defines no dynamical quantity.

contents.name: Section 1.3 'Newtonian Mechanics: Many Particles': F_i = sum_j F_ij + F_i^ext, Newton's third law, total mass and centre of mass with F_ext = M R-double-dot
contents.reason: The many-particle balance development, including the pair-force decomposition and the centre-of-mass theorem, is the subject of the balances pages of the track and requires their force postulates; it is not a prerequisite of the framework page.

contents.name: Section 3.1.1 path-ordered exponentials and angular velocity: the antisymmetric matrix Omega = R^T R-dot and its vector representation, with the moving-frame acceleration identity

sources.locator: Chapter 1 Sections 1.1-1.4, printed pages 2-10 (PDF pages 8-16); Chapter 6 Sections 6.1-6.2, printed pages 93-95 (PDF pages 99-101)

contents.name: Section 1.1 'Newton's Laws of Motion': a particle as an object of insignificant size, a reference frame as a choice of origin with Cartesian axes, the trajectory x(t), the definitions v = dx/dt and a = d^2x/dt^2, and the componentwise derivative of a vector-valued position
Section 1.1.1 'Newton's Laws': the three laws of motion as axioms of the framework
contents.reason: The force postulates and the equations of motion are the subject of the forces-and-initial-data page of the track; the framework page adopts only kinematics and asserts no force law.

contents.name: Section 1.2 'Inertial Frames and Newton's First Law' and Section 1.2.1 'Galilean Relativity': inertial frames are not unique; translations x' = x + a, rotations x' = R x with R^T R = 1 and boosts x' = x + v t map inertial frames to inertial frames; if d^2x/dt^2 = 0 holds in one frame it holds in the other; the transformations generate the Galilean group
Section 1.2.1 remark on the residual x' = lambda x rescalings of coordinates
contents.reason: Unit rescalings are handled as a dimension convention of the framework rather than as a frame transformation; no claim about absolute spatial scale is made or needed by any item of this pair.

contents.name: Section 1.3 'Newton's Second Law' and Section 1.4 'Looking Forwards: The Validity of Newtonian Mechanics'

Section 6.1-6.2 'Rotating Frames', 'Velocity and Acceleration in a Rotating Frame' and 'Newton's Equation of Motion in a Rotating Frame': equations (6.3) and (6.4) relating velocities and accelerations in inertial and rotating frames, and the three fictitious-force terms of (6.5)

sources.locator: Chapter 1 Sections 1.1-1.2 'Kinematics: Basic notions' and 'Dynamics: Newton's laws', chapter pages 1-3 (PDF pages 5-8)

contents.name: Section 1.1 points (i)-(v): Euclidean geometry notions, reference frames as a coordinate system plus a clock, absolute ('Newtonian') space and time with the Euclidean metric (1.2), the velocity (1.3) and acceleration (1.4), and the transfer of r, v, a between frames (1.5)-(1.7) with the caveat that mutual rotation makes the velocity and acceleration transfers more complicated
Section 1.1 point (vi): a particle as a localized object whose size and shape are negligible for the problem at hand

Section 1.2: the first Newton law as the postulate that an inertial frame exists in which a fully isolated particle moves with v = const, with all frames moving without rotation or acceleration relative to it inertial, and each particle characterized by a scalar constant mass m_k
Section 1.2: total momentum P = sum m_k v_k and its conservation for isolated systems, and the second and third laws in momentum form
contents.reason: Conservation of total momentum and the interaction laws are established on the balances pages of the track from their own force postulates; the framework page deliberately adopts no particle dynamics.

contents.name: Section 1.1: the configuration of a system of constituent point particles, the configuration space as the set of all configurations, its dimension as the number of degrees of freedom, and the worked statement that two point particles constrained to a fixed mutual distance have a five-dimensional configuration space

Section 1.2: generalized coordinates as parameters labelling configurations, the coordinate function chi, the coordinate path q = chi composed with the configuration path, and the generalized velocity Dq as the rate of change of the coordinate path
Section 1.4: the free-particle Lagrangian as the kinetic energy and its stationary-action role
contents.reason: The stationary-action and Lagrangian development belongs to the variational pages of the track, which supply the action functional, admissible variations and the Legendre transformation with their own hypotheses.
